sections.title: C1-M3-L2 — Éditoriaux et tribunes économiques : repérer la position et le ton de l'auteur
sections.contentHtml:
Objectifs :

  • Distinguer dans une tribune de 350 à 450 mots l'opinion de l'auteur des points de vue qu'il rapporte pour les discuter.
  • Qualifier le ton d'un éditorial (sceptique, ironique, mesuré, alarmiste, conciliant) à l'aide d'au moins deux indices textuels.
  • Expliquer le sens en contexte d'au moins quatre expressions idiomatiques de la presse économique, avec au moins 75 % de réponses correctes aux QCM.

Compétence C2 — niveau C1.2 — 40 min

L'éditorial (editorial, leader) exprime la position d'un journal ; la tribune (op-ed, opinion piece, column) celle d'un auteur extérieur ou d'un chroniqueur. Dans les deux cas, le texte cherche à convaincre, et les questions de niveau C1 portent rarement sur les faits : elles portent sur la position, le ton et les sous-entendus.

1. Qui parle ? Un auteur cite souvent des avis qu'il ne partage pas pour mieux les réfuter : Critics argue that…, Proponents claim…, We are told that…, The conventional wisdom is that…. Le verbe introducteur est un indice précieux : claim et insist prennent souvent de la distance, alors que show et demonstrate valident l'affirmation. Ne confondez jamais l'opinion rapportée avec celle de l'auteur : c'est le piège le plus fréquent.

2. La structure concession-réfutation. Of course, … / To be fair, … / Granted, … introduit une concession ; But / Yet / Even so annonce la thèse réelle. Exemple : To be fair, the trial produced some encouraging results. Yet a six-month pilot in a handful of firms proves very little. L'auteur reconnaît un point, puis le relativise : il est sceptique.

3. Le ton. Il se lit dans :

  • les adjectifs et adverbes évaluatifs (a welcome step, a deeply flawed plan, conveniently, predictably) ;
  • l'ironie (Shareholders will no doubt be thrilled to learn that…) : le sens réel est l'inverse du sens littéral ;
  • les questions rhétoriques (Who, exactly, benefits?), qui n'attendent pas de réponse mais orientent le lecteur ;
  • l'intensité du lexique : un ton mesuré (it is not obvious that…) n'est pas un ton virulent (this is reckless).

4. Les expressions idiomatiques. La presse économique en est riche : to kick the can down the road (repousser un problème), a sticking plaster ou band-aid solution (une solution provisoire), to throw good money after bad (s'entêter à investir à perte), the elephant in the room (le problème dont personne ne parle), a race to the bottom (une surenchère à la baisse), to have one's cake and eat it (vouloir le beurre et l'argent du beurre). Le contexte permet toujours de vérifier le sens.

5. Les options pièges. Dans les QCM, méfiez-vous des réponses qui attribuent à l'auteur une position extrême alors que le texte est nuancé (« l'auteur rejette totalement… » quand il émet des réserves), ou qui reprennent l'avis d'un tiers cité. Pour la question « What is the author's main point? », cherchez la phrase qui revient en conclusion : les tribunes reformulent presque toujours leur thèse dans le dernier paragraphe.

Méthode : lisez le titre et la dernière phrase en premier (thèse probable), soulignez les verbes introducteurs et les connecteurs de concession, puis répondez dans l'ordre du texte en justifiant chaque choix par une citation.

Langue clé

AnglaisFrançaisUsage
Critics argue that the scheme is too costly.Les détracteurs estiment que le dispositif est trop coûteux.opinion rapportée, pas forcément celle de l'auteur
To be fair, the results were encouraging. Yet…Pour être honnête, les résultats étaient encourageants. Pourtant…concession suivie de la thèse réelle
Who, exactly, stands to gain from this?Qui, au juste, a quelque chose à y gagner ?question rhétorique qui oriente le lecteur
Investors will no doubt be delighted to hear that…Les investisseurs seront sans doute ravis d'apprendre que…ironie : le sens réel est l'inverse
It is far from obvious that this will work.Il est loin d'être évident que cela fonctionne.scepticisme exprimé de manière mesurée
This merely kicks the can down the road.Cela ne fait que repousser le problème.critique d'une solution qui retarde une décision

Vocabulaire

TermeTraductionExemple
op-edtribune (texte d'opinion signé)The CEO published an op-ed defending the merger.
leader (UK)éditorialToday's leader calls for tighter rules on buybacks.
conventional wisdomidée reçue, opinion dominanteThe conventional wisdom is that remote work hurts productivity.
to kick the can down the roadrepousser un problème à plus tardThe budget simply kicks the can down the road.
sticking plastersolution provisoire, rustineThe subsidy is a sticking plaster, not a cure.
to throw good money after bads'entêter à investir à perteRescuing the project again would be throwing good money after bad.
the elephant in the roomle problème que personne n'ose aborderProductivity is the elephant in the room.
a race to the bottomun nivellement par le basTax competition has become a race to the bottom.
to have one's cake and eat itvouloir le beurre et l'argent du beurreFirms want flexibility and loyalty: they want to have their cake and eat it.
short-termismcourt-termismeShort-termism undermines long-term investment.
disingenuoushypocrite, de mauvaise foiIt is disingenuous to call this a pay rise.
to pay lip service todéfendre du bout des lèvresMany boards pay lip service to diversity.
a welcome stepune avancée bienvenueThe new disclosure rule is a welcome step.
scathingcinglant, virulentThe column was a scathing attack on the board.

Dialogue : Revue de presse du lundi : ce que pense vraiment l'éditorialiste

Service communication d'un groupe industriel à Manchester. Le responsable des relations presse fait la revue des tribunes du week-end avec une chargée de veille.

PersonnageRépliqueTraduction
Oliver BrandtSo, Amara, the column on the four-day week. Is the writer for it or against it?Alors, Amara, la chronique sur la semaine de quatre jours. L'auteur est pour ou contre ?
Amara NwosuAt first I thought he was in favour. He spends two paragraphs on the positive results.Au début, j'ai cru qu'il était pour. Il consacre deux paragraphes aux résultats positifs.
Oliver BrandtAnd then?Et ensuite ?
Amara NwosuThen comes 'Yet a six-month pilot in thirty firms proves very little.' That's his real position.Puis vient « Pourtant, un pilote de six mois dans trente entreprises ne prouve pas grand-chose ». C'est sa vraie position.
Oliver BrandtClassic concession. He gives the other side its due, then dismantles it.Concession classique. Il reconnaît ce qui revient au camp adverse, puis le démonte.
Amara NwosuExactly. And he says supporters 'insist' the gains are lasting, not that they've shown it.Exactement. Et il dit que les partisans « affirment » que les gains sont durables, pas qu'ils l'ont démontré.
Oliver BrandtGood catch. The reporting verb tells you where he stands. What about the leader on buybacks?Bien vu. Le verbe introducteur montre où il se situe. Et l'éditorial sur les rachats d'actions ?
Amara NwosuMuch harsher. 'Shareholders will no doubt be thrilled' — but the context makes it clear it's ironic.Beaucoup plus dur. « Les actionnaires seront sans doute ravis » — mais le contexte montre clairement que c'est ironique.
Oliver BrandtWould you call it scathing, or just critical?Tu le qualifierais de cinglant, ou simplement de critique ?
Amara NwosuScathing. It calls the policy 'a sticking plaster on a broken leg'.Cinglant. Il qualifie la politique de « pansement sur une jambe cassée ».
Oliver BrandtFair enough. Does it mention us directly?D'accord. Est-ce qu'il nous cite directement ?
Amara NwosuNot by name, but it refers to 'one Midlands manufacturer' that cut research spending. Everyone will know who that is.Pas nommément, mais il évoque « un industriel des Midlands » qui a réduit ses dépenses de recherche. Tout le monde saura de qui il s'agit.
Oliver BrandtThen that's the elephant in the room for tomorrow's board briefing. Flag it in red.Alors c'est le sujet qui fâche pour le point du conseil de demain. Signale-le en rouge.
Amara NwosuWill do. I'll quote the exact sentences so nobody accuses us of overreacting.Entendu. Je citerai les phrases exactes pour qu'on ne nous accuse pas de surréagir.

Exercices corrigés

Exercice 1 — C1-M3-L2-I1 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez cette tribune parue dans un magazine économique et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

The four-day week deserves better evidence — not more applause
by Gregory Ashworth, contributing columnist

Few workplace ideas have enjoyed a warmer press than the four-day week. When the results of the latest pilot were published last month, the headlines wrote themselves: productivity maintained, sick days down, staff happier, and almost nine in ten participating firms planning to continue. Proponents insist that the case is now closed.

To be fair, the findings are genuinely encouraging, and anyone who has worked a fifty-hour week will understand the appeal. It would be churlish to dismiss the testimony of managers who say their teams have become more focused, or of employees who describe finally having time for their children. Those benefits are real, and they matter.

Yet a six-month pilot involving thirty-one self-selected companies proves very little about the economy as a whole. The firms that volunteered were overwhelmingly small, office-based and already inclined to experiment. Their staff knew they were being observed, and knew that the scheme would continue only if the numbers looked good. Under those conditions, a burst of enthusiasm is hardly surprising. Whether it survives the second winter, the first recession or the departure of the founder who championed it is another question entirely.

Nor does the pilot tell us much about the sectors where most people actually work. A hospital ward, a warehouse or a primary school cannot simply compress five days of service into four. For them, a shorter week means either hiring more staff or reducing the service — and somebody has to pay for both.

None of this means the idea should be abandoned. It means that policymakers who are now talking about encouraging the four-day week through tax incentives are getting ahead of the evidence. What we need is a longer, larger and less flattering study: one that includes firms that did not ask to take part, that runs for at least two years and that measures output rather than satisfaction.

The four-day week may well turn out to be one of the great reforms of our working lives. If so, it will survive a rigorous test. If it cannot, better to find out before the public purse is committed.

1. In the first paragraph, the word “insist” suggests that the columnist
A. fully shares the supporters' conclusion.
B. has reservations about the supporters' claim.
C. considers the pilot results to be false.
D. is reporting a view held by most economists.

2. What is the function of the second paragraph?
A. To concede real benefits before questioning the conclusions.
B. To show that the columnist has changed his mind about the four-day week since the pilot results were published.
C. To criticise managers for exaggerating the benefits.
D. To present the opinion of employees who oppose the scheme.

3. Why does the columnist mention that staff “knew they were being observed”?
A. To accuse the participating firms of falsifying their data.
B. To explain why many employees were reluctant to take part in the trial in the first place.
C. To suggest that the conditions of the trial may have inflated the positive results.
D. To argue that the scheme should be extended to other sectors.

4. What is the columnist's attitude to the idea of tax incentives?
A. He considers them a sensible way to test the idea.
B. He believes they should be reserved for hospitals and schools.
C. He thinks they would be the best way to finance extra staff.
D. He regards them as premature given the current evidence.

5. Which statement best summarises the columnist's overall position?
A. The four-day week has failed and should be abandoned.
B. The idea is promising but untested so far.
C. The four-day week works only in the public sector.
D. The four-day week should be made compulsory for all firms once a two-year study has been completed.

Corrigé

1. B — has reservations about the supporters' claim.. « insist » est un verbe introducteur qui prend ses distances : les partisans affirment avec force que la question est tranchée, ce que l'auteur va discuter. Il ne dit pas pour autant que les résultats sont faux (« the findings are genuinely encouraging »).
2. A — To concede real benefits before questioning the conclusions.. « To be fair… It would be churlish to dismiss… » est une concession : l'auteur reconnaît les bénéfices avant le « Yet » du paragraphe suivant. Il ne critique pas les managers : il juge « churlish » (mesquin) de rejeter leur témoignage.
3. C — To suggest that the conditions of the trial may have inflated the positive results.. Être observé, savoir que la suite dépend des chiffres : « a burst of enthusiasm is hardly surprising ». L'auteur suggère un biais, sans accuser quiconque de fraude, ce qui serait une lecture excessive.
4. D — He regards them as premature given the current evidence.. « getting ahead of the evidence » = aller plus vite que les preuves disponibles : il juge ces incitations prématurées. Il ne les rejette pas définitivement, il demande d'abord une étude plus rigoureuse.
5. B — The idea is promising but untested so far.. La conclusion réunit les deux faces : « may well turn out to be one of the great reforms » mais doit « survive a rigorous test ». « None of this means the idea should be abandoned » écarte explicitement la première option.

Exercice 2 — C1-M3-L2-I2 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez l'éditorial et répondez aux questions. Attention à l'ironie et aux questions rhétoriques.

Leader: Buy now, invest later

Another reporting season, another wave of share buybacks. Last quarter, the twenty largest listed manufacturers in the country announced plans to repurchase almost £14 billion of their own shares — more than they intend to spend on research and development over the next two years combined. Shareholders will no doubt be thrilled. Whether the economy should be is a different matter.

The case for buybacks is familiar. A company with surplus cash and no attractive projects, the argument runs, should return that money to its owners rather than squander it on vanity acquisitions. In principle, this is perfectly sound. Capital that sits idle on a balance sheet helps nobody, and investors are often better placed than managers to decide where it should go next.

But how many of these companies genuinely have no attractive projects? The same boards that are now returning billions have spent the past three years warning that they lack the capacity to meet demand, that their plants are ageing and that skills shortages are holding back output. One Midlands manufacturer cut its research budget by a fifth last year while simultaneously launching its largest ever buyback. Such firms cannot have it both ways: either there is nothing worth investing in, or there is and they are choosing not to.

The suspicion, which is hard to shake, is that the timing has less to do with capital discipline than with executive pay. When bonuses are linked to earnings per share, reducing the number of shares is the quickest way to make the figure rise. It requires no new customers, no new products and no risk — except, of course, to the long-term health of the business.

None of this calls for a ban. Buybacks have a legitimate place, and politicians who propose taxing them punitively are offering a sticking plaster on a broken leg. What is needed is transparency. Boards should be required to explain, in plain language, why repurchasing shares is a better use of capital than investing in their own operations, and remuneration committees should strip the mechanical effect of buybacks out of bonus calculations. If the case is as strong as companies claim, they should have no difficulty making it.

1. How should the sentence “Shareholders will no doubt be thrilled” be understood?
A. As sincere praise for the companies' generosity.
B. As evidence that shareholders requested the buybacks.
C. As an ironic remark that prepares a criticism.
D. As a prediction that share prices will fall.

2. In the second paragraph, the writer
A. presents the opposing argument and accepts that it is valid in theory.
B. explains why buybacks should be banned.
C. argues that investors always make better decisions than managers.
D. criticises companies that make vanity acquisitions.

3. What is the purpose of the question “But how many of these companies genuinely have no attractive projects?”
A. To ask readers to send examples of attractive projects.
B. To admit that the writer lacks reliable information about the companies' investment plans.
C. To imply most of them have worthwhile projects.
D. To praise companies for their caution.

4. What does the writer imply about executive pay?
A. It is too low to attract good managers.
B. It may encourage managers to favour buybacks for their own benefit.
C. It has no connection with the timing of buybacks.
D. It should be paid entirely in shares.

5. What does the writer recommend?
A. A heavy tax on all share buybacks, as proposed by several politicians, to discourage them.
B. A complete ban on buybacks for manufacturers.
C. Higher research budgets imposed by law.
D. Transparency and adjusted bonus rules.

Corrigé

1. C — As an ironic remark that prepares a criticism.. La phrase suivante (« Whether the economy should be is a different matter ») révèle l'ironie : le ravissement des actionnaires est opposé à l'intérêt général. Il ne s'agit pas d'un éloge sincère.
2. A — presents the opposing argument and accepts that it is valid in theory.. « The argument runs » introduit l'argument des partisans, puis « In principle, this is perfectly sound » le valide en théorie, avant le « But » du paragraphe 3. « always » est trop fort : le texte dit « often better placed ».
3. C — To imply most of them have worthwhile projects.. C'est une question rhétorique : la suite (capacités insuffisantes, usines vieillissantes) montre que ces entreprises ont des besoins d'investissement. Elle n'appelle pas de réponse et n'exprime pas une ignorance.
4. B — It may encourage managers to favour buybacks for their own benefit.. « The suspicion… is that the timing has less to do with capital discipline than with executive pay » : les bonus indexés sur le bénéfice par action incitent à racheter des actions. L'auteur parle de soupçon, sans affirmer de fraude.
5. D — Transparency and adjusted bonus rules.. « What is needed is transparency » : explication en langage clair et neutralisation de l'effet mécanique sur les bonus. La taxation punitive est qualifiée de « sticking plaster on a broken leg » (solution dérisoire), et l'interdiction est écartée (« None of this calls for a ban »).

Exercice 3 — C1-M3-L2-I3 (C2, C1.1)

Lisez cette chronique et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

The empty office is not the end of the city centre
by Leah Montgomery, urban economics correspondent

Walk through the business district of almost any large city on a Friday afternoon and the conclusion seems obvious. The cafés are half empty, the lifts are quiet and the “To Let” signs multiply by the month. Office vacancy rates have reached levels not seen in two decades, and several property funds have quietly written down the value of their portfolios. The conventional wisdom is that hybrid working has dealt the traditional city centre a fatal blow.

I am not convinced. Not because the problems are imaginary — they are not — but because this narrative confuses a change in how offices are used with the disappearance of the need for them. Demand for the best buildings, those with good transport links, generous natural light and decent energy ratings, has barely fallen. Rents for such space have, in some cities, actually risen. The pain is concentrated in older, poorly insulated blocks that were already struggling to find tenants before anyone had heard of video calls.

In other words, what we are witnessing looks less like a collapse than a sorting. Companies are using their newfound flexibility to trade down in size and up in quality. That is bad news for owners of mediocre buildings, but it is not necessarily bad news for cities.

The real question is what happens to the space left behind. Converting offices into homes is often proposed as the answer, and in some cases it will be. But the economics are tougher than enthusiasts admit: deep floor plates leave interiors without daylight, and the cost of new plumbing and fire safety work can exceed the value of the finished flats. Councils that simply relax planning rules and wait for developers to step in may find themselves waiting for a long time.

Cities that thrive will be those that treat the current upheaval as an opportunity to rethink their centres as places to live, learn and spend time — not merely as places to commute to. That requires patient public investment and a willingness to accept that the business district of 2040 will look rather different from the one we knew. It does not require a funeral.

1. What is the “conventional wisdom” mentioned in the first paragraph?
A. That property funds have been overvaluing their office portfolios for a number of years.
B. That hybrid working has done irreparable damage to city centres.
C. That office vacancy rates will soon return to normal.
D. That cafés are the first businesses to suffer in a downturn.

2. What distinction does the writer draw in the second paragraph?
A. Between offices in large cities and offices in small towns.
B. Between companies that use video calls and those that do not.
C. Between a change in how offices are used and the end of the need for offices.
D. Between the views of property owners and those of tenants.

3. What does the writer mean by “a sorting”?
A. Firms are trading down in size and up in quality.
B. Councils are deciding which buildings should be demolished.
C. Employees are choosing between working from home and returning to the office, depending on the day of the week.
D. Property funds are selling their best buildings first.

4. What is the writer's attitude towards converting offices into homes?
A. She rejects it as completely unrealistic.
B. She sees it as the main solution to the crisis.
C. She believes developers are already rushing to convert offices now that planning rules have been relaxed.
D. She sees it as useful but tougher than claimed.

Corrigé

1. B — That hybrid working has done irreparable damage to city centres.. L'idée dominante est que le travail hybride a porté « a fatal blow » (un coup fatal) aux centres-villes. C'est la thèse que l'autrice va contester avec « I am not convinced ».
2. C — Between a change in how offices are used and the end of the need for offices.. Elle reproche au discours dominant de confondre « a change in how offices are used with the disappearance of the need for them ». La suite (bons immeubles toujours demandés) illustre cette distinction.
3. A — Firms are trading down in size and up in quality.. « sorting » = un tri : les entreprises « trade down in size and up in quality », au détriment des immeubles médiocres. Le texte ne parle ni de démolitions décidées par les collectivités ni de ventes des meilleurs actifs.
4. D — She sees it as useful but tougher than claimed.. « in some cases it will be. But the economics are tougher than enthusiasts admit » : position nuancée, ni rejet total ni adhésion. La remarque finale sur les collectivités qui pourraient « wait for a long time » contredit l'idée d'un afflux de promoteurs.

Exercice 4 — C1-M3-L2-I4 (C2, C1.2)

Complétez cet extrait de tribune avec l'expression idiomatique qui convient.

For years, ministers have preferred to [1] _____ rather than confront the funding gap in social care. The latest emergency grant is yet another [2] _____: it will keep services afloat until the spring, but it does nothing to address the underlying problem. Everyone at the summit talked about efficiency, yet nobody mentioned the [3] _____: the sector simply cannot recruit enough staff. Pouring further subsidies into failing providers without reform would be [4] _____. And competition between regions to offer the lowest fees risks becoming [5] _____.

[1] cut corners / bite the bullet / turn the tables / kick the can down the road

[2] silver lining / level playing field / sticking plaster / blank cheque

[3] tip of the iceberg / elephant in the room / bottom line / grey area

[4] throwing good money after bad / cashing in / breaking even / money well spent

[5] a win-win situation / a learning curve / a game changer / a race to the bottom

Corrigé

[1] kick the can down the road. « kick the can down the road » = repousser un problème, ce que confirme « rather than confront ». « bite the bullet » signifierait au contraire affronter la difficulté.
[2] sticking plaster. « sticking plaster » = solution provisoire : elle tient jusqu'au printemps sans traiter le fond. « blank cheque » (carte blanche) ne correspond pas à une aide ponctuelle.
[3] elephant in the room. « the elephant in the room » = le problème évident dont personne ne parle (« nobody mentioned »). « tip of the iceberg » désignerait la partie visible d'un problème plus large.
[4] throwing good money after bad. « throwing good money after bad » = continuer à investir dans ce qui échoue. « money well spent » serait contraire à la position critique de l'auteur.
[5] a race to the bottom. « a race to the bottom » = une surenchère à la baisse (ici, des tarifs toujours plus bas). « a win-win situation » contredit le verbe « risks ».

title: C1-M3 — Études de marché et livres blancs : données, interprétations et intérêts
description: Distinguer dans une synthèse d'étude de marché de 350 à 450 mots les données mesurées, les estimations et les interprétations des auteurs. Repérer au moins deux limites méthodologiques (échantillon, déclaratif, corrélation) signalées ou passées sous silence par un document. Identifier l'intérêt commercial d'un livre blanc et son effet sur la présentation des résultats, avec au moins 75 % de réponses correctes aux QCM.
imageQuery: business English Études de marché et livres blancs : données, interprétations et intérêts

sections.title: C1-M3-L3 — Études de marché et livres blancs : données, interprétations et intérêts
sections.contentHtml:
Objectifs :

  • Distinguer dans une synthèse d'étude de marché de 350 à 450 mots les données mesurées, les estimations et les interprétations des auteurs.
  • Repérer au moins deux limites méthodologiques (échantillon, déclaratif, corrélation) signalées ou passées sous silence par un document.
  • Identifier l'intérêt commercial d'un livre blanc et son effet sur la présentation des résultats, avec au moins 75 % de réponses correctes aux QCM.

Compétence C2 — niveau C1.1 — 40 min

Les études de marché (market research reports) et les livres blancs (white papers) sont des documents longs, souvent truffés de chiffres. Au niveau C1, il ne suffit pas de retrouver un pourcentage : il faut savoir d'où il vient, ce qu'il mesure vraiment et qui a intérêt à le présenter ainsi.

1. Données, estimations, projections. Distinguez :

  • les données observées (sales rose by 12% in 2025) ;
  • les estimations (we estimate the market at €2.1 billion) ;
  • les projections (the market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 9% to 2030). Une projection repose sur des hypothèses (assuming…, based on current trends) : si l'hypothèse change, le chiffre tombe.

2. La méthodologie. Cherchez la taille et la nature de l'échantillon (a sample of 1,200 respondents, self-selected, representative of), le mode de collecte (online survey, in-depth interviews), et le caractère déclaratif des réponses (self-reported). Ce que les gens disent qu'ils feront (say they would consider) n'est pas ce qu'ils font. Les mises en garde (caveats) sont souvent placées discrètement : figures should be treated as indicative, caution is advised when….

3. Corrélation n'est pas causalité. Companies that use X report higher margins ne prouve pas que X augmente les marges : les entreprises les plus rentables ont peut-être simplement plus de moyens pour adopter X. Les auteurs prudents l'écrivent (this does not establish a causal link) ; les auteurs intéressés le laissent entendre.

4. Le livre blanc, document d'influence. Un white paper publié par un éditeur de logiciels ou un cabinet de conseil vise souvent à créer un besoin. Indices : définition très large du problème, chiffres spectaculaires sans source (up to 40% savings), formules floues (leading organisations, industry experts agree), puis présentation de la solution… de l'auteur. Le mot up to est particulièrement trompeur : il désigne un maximum, pas une moyenne.

5. Vocabulaire utile. Addressable market (marché adressable), penetration rate (taux de pénétration), year-on-year (sur un an), uptake (adoption), respondents (personnes interrogées), margin of error (marge d'erreur), outlier (valeur aberrante), headline figure (chiffre phare).

Pièges des QCM. Une option peut citer un chiffre exact du texte mais l'attribuer à la mauvaise population (all buyers au lieu de buyers under 35) ou transformer une intention en fait. Une autre peut prêter aux auteurs une certitude qu'ils n'ont pas. Vérifiez toujours : qui a été interrogé, sur quoi, et avec quelle prudence la conclusion est formulée.

Dernier réflexe : lorsqu'une question porte sur « the author's purpose », demandez-vous qui a commandé ou publié le document. La réponse change souvent la lecture de tout le texte.

Langue clé

AnglaisFrançaisUsage
The market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 9% to 2030.Le marché devrait croître à un taux annuel moyen de 9 % jusqu'en 2030.projection reposant sur des hypothèses
Figures should be treated as indicative.Les chiffres sont à considérer comme indicatifs.mise en garde méthodologique
This does not establish a causal link.Cela n'établit pas de lien de causalité.prudence sur l'interprétation d'une corrélation
Respondents say they would consider switching.Les répondants déclarent qu'ils envisageraient de changer.intention déclarée, pas comportement observé
Savings of up to 40% have been reported.Des économies allant jusqu'à 40 % ont été signalées.maximum présenté comme argument : à lire avec prudence
Based on a sample of 1,200 decision-makers…Sur la base d'un échantillon de 1 200 décideurs…présentation de la méthodologie

Vocabulaire

TermeTraductionExemple
addressable marketmarché adressableThe addressable market is estimated at €2.1 billion.
compound annual growth rate (CAGR)taux de croissance annuel composéAnalysts forecast a CAGR of 9% to 2030.
respondentpersonne interrogée, répondantForty per cent of respondents were based in Germany.
self-reporteddéclaratif (déclaré par l'intéressé)Self-reported usage tends to be overstated.
sampleéchantillonThe sample was weighted by age and region.
margin of errormarge d'erreurThe margin of error is plus or minus three points.
caveatmise en garde, réserveThe report contains several important caveats.
uptakeadoption, taux de recoursUptake among small firms remains low.
penetration ratetaux de pénétrationThe penetration rate reached 14% in urban areas.
year-on-yearsur un an, en glissement annuelSales rose 8% year-on-year.
outliervaleur aberrante, cas atypiqueWe excluded two outliers from the analysis.
headline figurechiffre phare, chiffre mis en avantThe headline figure hides large regional differences.
vested interestintérêt personnel en jeuThe vendor has a vested interest in the findings.
to extrapolateextrapolerIt is risky to extrapolate from such a small sample.

Dialogue : Peut-on se fier à ce livre blanc ?

Bureau des achats d'un fabricant de composants à Lyon, en visioconférence avec une consultante britannique. Ils évaluent un livre blanc reçu d'un éditeur de logiciels.

PersonnageRépliqueTraduction
Thomas KellerRachel, thanks for reading the white paper. Our operations team is very excited by the 40% figure.Rachel, merci d'avoir lu le livre blanc. Notre équipe d'exploitation est très enthousiaste devant le chiffre de 40 %.
Rachel WhitmoreI'm not surprised. It's in large print on page one. But look at the wording: 'savings of up to 40%'.Ça ne m'étonne pas. Il est en gros caractères en page un. Mais regardez la formulation : « des économies allant jusqu'à 40 % ».
Thomas KellerSo that's the best case, not the average.Donc c'est le meilleur cas, pas la moyenne.
Rachel WhitmoreExactly. And there's no indication of how many sites achieved it. It might be one plant out of fifty.Exactement. Et rien n'indique combien de sites l'ont atteint. Ce pourrait être une usine sur cinquante.
Thomas KellerWhat about the survey? They say 78% of leading manufacturers plan to adopt predictive maintenance.Et l'enquête ? Ils disent que 78 % des industriels de pointe prévoient d'adopter la maintenance prédictive.
Rachel WhitmoreTwo problems. 'Leading manufacturers' isn't defined, and 'plan to adopt' is an intention, not a purchase.Deux problèmes. « Industriels de pointe » n'est pas défini, et « prévoient d'adopter » est une intention, pas un achat.
Thomas KellerAnd who carried out the survey?Et qui a réalisé l'enquête ?
Rachel WhitmoreThe vendor itself, among its own customers and webinar attendees. Hardly a neutral sample.L'éditeur lui-même, auprès de ses propres clients et des participants à ses webinaires. Un échantillon guère neutre.
Thomas KellerSo should we just ignore the document?Alors, faut-il simplement ignorer le document ?
Rachel WhitmoreNo, the technical section is actually solid. The problem is the marketing wrapped around it.Non, la partie technique est en fait solide. Le problème, c'est l'emballage marketing autour.
Thomas KellerThen what would you need to see before trusting the savings figure?Alors, que vous faudrait-il pour faire confiance au chiffre d'économies ?
Rachel WhitmoreThe median result across all sites, the baseline they compared against, and two references we can call ourselves.Le résultat médian sur l'ensemble des sites, la situation de référence utilisée et deux références que nous pouvons appeler nous-mêmes.
Thomas KellerThat's a reasonable request. I'll put it in writing before the demo next week.C'est une demande raisonnable. Je la formulerai par écrit avant la démonstration de la semaine prochaine.
Rachel WhitmoreGood. If they can't provide it, that tells you something too.Bien. S'ils ne peuvent pas la fournir, cela vous apprendra aussi quelque chose.

Exercices corrigés

Exercice 1 — C1-M3-L3-I1 (C2, C1.1)

Lisez la synthèse d'une étude de marché et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

Executive Summary
E-bike Subscription Services in Northern Europe — Market Assessment 2026
Prepared by Kestrel Analytics for internal circulation

Subscription models, under which customers pay a monthly fee for the use, maintenance and insurance of an electric bicycle, remain a small but fast-growing segment of the urban mobility market. We estimate that around 310,000 subscriptions were active across the six countries covered by this study at the end of 2025, up 38% year-on-year. Germany and the Netherlands together account for almost two thirds of the total.

Our central scenario projects the number of active subscriptions to reach 1.1 million by 2030, implying a compound annual growth rate of roughly 29%. This projection assumes that employer-sponsored schemes, which currently benefit from favourable tax treatment in three of the six countries, continue in their present form. Should these incentives be withdrawn or significantly reduced, growth would be considerably slower; our low scenario, presented in Section 5, puts the 2030 figure at around 600,000.

The consumer survey conducted for this report (2,400 respondents aged 18–65 living in cities of more than 200,000 inhabitants) suggests substantial latent demand: 27% of respondents said they would consider subscribing to an e-bike service within the next two years. Experience from comparable markets indicates, however, that stated intentions of this kind convert into actual subscriptions at a rate well below one in five, and we have adjusted our forecasts accordingly.

Competition is intensifying. The three largest providers control an estimated 55% of the market, but several well-funded entrants launched in 2025, and price competition has already compressed average monthly fees by around 8%. We expect consolidation over the next three years, as smaller operators struggle to finance fleet renewal and maintenance networks.

Finally, we would stress that reliable data on churn remain scarce. Providers disclose little about how long customers keep their subscriptions, and the estimates used in this report are derived from a limited number of interviews with industry participants. Readers should therefore treat the profitability analysis in Section 7 as indicative rather than definitive.

1. What does the first paragraph tell us about the market at the end of 2025?
A. It was already the largest segment of urban mobility.
B. It was still modest in size but expanding rapidly.
C. It was evenly distributed across the six countries.
D. It had grown by 38% since the start of the decade.

2. On what does the central scenario mainly depend?
A. The continuation of tax advantages for employer-sponsored schemes.
B. A sharp fall in the price of electric bicycles.
C. The withdrawal of several competitors from the market.
D. The results of the consumer survey alone.

3. How do the authors treat the finding that 27% of respondents would consider subscribing?
A. They use it directly as a forecast of future subscriptions.
B. They reject it because the sample was too small.
C. They see it as an intention, only partly convertible.
D. They consider it proof that the number of subscriptions will at least triple by 2030.

4. What do the authors expect to happen to smaller operators?
A. They will gain market share thanks to lower prices.
B. They will receive public funding to help them renew their fleets and maintenance networks.
C. They will form a joint maintenance network.
D. Some will probably disappear or be taken over.

5. What is the purpose of the last paragraph?
A. To warn readers that part of the analysis rests on limited evidence.
B. To criticise providers for publishing misleading churn figures.
C. To announce that the profitability analysis has been removed.
D. To prove that customers keep their subscriptions for several years.

Corrigé

1. B — It was still modest in size but expanding rapidly.. « a small but fast-growing segment » et +38 % sur un an. Le piège porte sur « year-on-year » : la hausse de 38 % est sur un an, pas depuis le début de la décennie ; l'Allemagne et les Pays-Bas concentrent près des deux tiers, la répartition n'est donc pas homogène.
2. A — The continuation of tax advantages for employer-sponsored schemes.. « This projection assumes that employer-sponsored schemes… continue in their present form ». Sans ces avantages fiscaux, c'est le scénario bas (environ 600 000) qui s'appliquerait.
3. C — They see it as an intention, only partly convertible.. Les intentions déclarées se transforment en abonnements « at a rate well below one in five », et les prévisions ont été « adjusted accordingly ». Ils ne rejettent pas l'enquête (2 400 répondants) mais en relativisent la portée.
4. D — Some will probably disappear or be taken over.. « We expect consolidation… as smaller operators struggle to finance fleet renewal » : la consolidation implique rachats ou disparitions. Aucun financement public ni réseau commun n'est évoqué.
5. A — To warn readers that part of the analysis rests on limited evidence.. C'est une mise en garde (caveat) : données de résiliation rares, estimations fondées sur peu d'entretiens, analyse à traiter « as indicative rather than definitive ». Les fournisseurs publient peu, mais ils ne sont pas accusés de publier des chiffres trompeurs.

Exercice 2 — C1-M3-L3-I2 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez cet extrait de livre blanc publié par un éditeur de logiciels et répondez aux questions. Soyez attentif à l'intérêt de l'auteur.

White Paper — The Hidden Cost of Unplanned Downtime
Published by Veltrix Software Ltd

Every minute a production line stands idle costs money. Yet many manufacturers still have only a vague idea of how much. In our experience working with industrial clients across Europe, unplanned downtime is one of the most significant and least understood drains on profitability in modern manufacturing.

Industry estimates vary widely, but some studies put the cost of an hour of unplanned downtime in automotive assembly at more than €1 million. Even in less capital-intensive sectors, the combined impact of lost output, overtime, expedited shipping and contractual penalties can quickly run into tens of thousands of euros per incident. Crucially, these costs are rarely captured in a single budget line, which explains why so many organisations underestimate them.

To understand how manufacturers are responding, Veltrix surveyed 640 operations and maintenance managers in the first quarter of 2026. Respondents were drawn from our customer base and from registered participants in our webinar series. Seventy-eight per cent of respondents at leading organisations said they intend to adopt predictive maintenance within three years, and those already using such tools reported fewer breakdowns than those relying on scheduled maintenance alone.

The benefits can be substantial. Clients using the Veltrix Predict platform have reported savings of up to 40% on maintenance costs and reductions of up to 50% in unplanned downtime. By combining sensor data with machine-learning models, the platform identifies the early signs of equipment failure, allowing interventions to be planned during scheduled stops rather than in the middle of a production run.

Of course, technology alone is not enough. Successful programmes depend on reliable data, clear ownership and the active involvement of maintenance teams, who sometimes view predictive tools with suspicion. Organisations that invest in training and change management are, in our experience, those that realise value most quickly.

The question for manufacturers is no longer whether to adopt predictive maintenance, but how quickly they can do so before competitors gain an advantage. To find out how much downtime is costing your plant, book a free assessment with one of our specialists.

1. What is the main purpose of the second paragraph?
A. To give precise figures for the reader's own sector.
B. To show that downtime costs are already well measured by most firms.
C. To make the problem appear large and underestimated.
D. To compare the automotive sector with other industries in detail.

2. What weakness in the survey can be inferred from the text?
A. The number of respondents was far too low for the results to be statistically meaningful.
B. The respondents were likely to be favourably disposed towards the publisher.
C. The survey was carried out before predictive maintenance existed.
D. Only automotive manufacturers were included.

3. Why should the claim that users of predictive tools “reported fewer breakdowns” be treated with caution?
A. Because breakdowns cannot be measured objectively.
B. Because the tools were tested only in laboratory conditions rather than in real production plants.
C. Because the figure contradicts the 78% intention rate.
D. Because it shows correlation, not causation.

4. In the fourth paragraph, what does the expression “up to 40%” indicate?
A. The best result observed, not a typical one.
B. The average saving achieved by all clients.
C. A guaranteed minimum saving for new clients.
D. The saving that clients can expect on average after three years of using the platform.

Corrigé

1. C — To make the problem appear large and underestimated.. Le paragraphe accumule des chiffres frappants (« more than €1 million ») et conclut que ces coûts sont sous-estimés : il construit le besoin. Les chiffres sont présentés comme variables (« Industry estimates vary widely »), pas précis pour le secteur du lecteur.
2. B — The respondents were likely to be favourably disposed towards the publisher.. L'échantillon est tiré de la clientèle de Veltrix et des inscrits à ses webinaires : un public déjà sensibilisé, probablement favorable. Le texte ne dit pas que 640 répondants est insuffisant, ni que seul l'automobile est concerné.
3. D — Because it shows correlation, not causation.. Les entreprises équipées ont peut-être d'autres avantages (moyens, organisation) : la comparaison ne prouve pas de causalité, et il s'agit en outre de données déclarées (« reported »). Le chiffre de 78 % concerne une intention et n'est pas contradictoire.
4. A — The best result observed, not a typical one.. « up to » désigne un plafond : le meilleur résultat, non la moyenne. C'est le piège classique du discours commercial ; rien n'indique combien de clients l'ont atteint.

Exercice 3 — C1-M3-L3-I3 (C2, C1.1)

Lisez l'extrait d'un rapport d'enquête sur les acheteurs professionnels et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

B2B Buying Behaviour Survey 2026 — Key Findings
Brightmoor Research Institute

  1. Digital channels now dominate the early stages of purchasing

Of the 1,850 procurement professionals surveyed, 71% said they complete more than half of their research before speaking to a supplier, compared with 58% in our 2023 survey. Buyers under 35 are the most independent: 84% of them prefer to shortlist suppliers without any contact with a sales representative. This does not, however, mean that sales teams have become irrelevant. Once a shortlist exists, two thirds of respondents still expect a detailed conversation with a specialist before committing to a contract worth more than €100,000.

  1. Peer recommendations outweigh vendor content

Asked which sources they trust most, respondents ranked recommendations from colleagues in other organisations first, followed by independent reviews. Vendor white papers and webinars came sixth out of eight. Interestingly, respondents who rated vendor content poorly were nevertheless frequent consumers of it, which suggests that such material is used for information gathering even when it is not trusted for decision-making.

  1. Firms with structured buying committees report higher satisfaction

Organisations in which purchases above a set threshold are reviewed by a cross-functional committee reported higher satisfaction with their suppliers than those in which decisions are taken by a single manager. We would caution against reading too much into this finding. Firms with formal committees tend to be larger and better resourced, and they may simply be in a stronger position to negotiate favourable terms. Our data do not allow us to isolate the effect of the committee itself.

  1. Sustainability criteria are rising, but slowly

Forty-three per cent of buyers said that environmental criteria were formally included in their supplier evaluations, up from 36% two years ago. However, only 12% reported that such criteria had been decisive in at least one contract award during the past year. The gap between policy and practice remains wide.

Methodology note: the survey was conducted online in January and February 2026 across nine European countries. Results have been weighted by company size and sector. The margin of error for the full sample is approximately ±2.3 percentage points.

1. According to section 1, what is true of buyers under 35?
A. They never speak to suppliers before signing a contract.
B. They make up 71% of the respondents.
C. They most often shortlist suppliers without salespeople.
D. They no longer expect any detailed conversation with a specialist, even for contracts above €100,000.

2. What do the authors find “interesting” in section 2?
A. Buyers consult vendor material frequently even though they do not trust it much.
B. Peer recommendations are rarely used in practice.
C. Vendor webinars are the most trusted source of information.
D. Independent reviews have become less popular since 2023.

3. What is the authors' attitude towards the finding in section 3?
A. They consider it proof that every firm should create a buying committee.
B. They are cautious, because other factors could explain the higher satisfaction.
C. They reject it as a statistical error.
D. They believe single managers negotiate better terms.

4. What does “The gap between policy and practice remains wide” mean in section 4?
A. Few companies have environmental policies at all.
B. Environmental criteria are already formally included in, and decisive for, the majority of contract awards made.
C. Buyers ignore their companies' policies on purpose.
D. Criteria are written down but rarely decisive.

Corrigé

1. C — They most often shortlist suppliers without salespeople.. 84 % des moins de 35 ans préfèrent établir leur liste restreinte sans commercial. Le chiffre de 71 % concerne l'ensemble des répondants ; et le texte précise que deux tiers attendent encore un échange avant un gros contrat.
2. A — Buyers consult vendor material frequently even though they do not trust it much.. Les répondants qui jugent mal les contenus des fournisseurs en sont pourtant de « frequent consumers » : ces contenus servent à s'informer, pas à décider. Les webinaires sont classés sixièmes sur huit.
3. B — They are cautious, because other factors could explain the higher satisfaction.. « We would caution against reading too much into this finding » : la taille et les moyens des entreprises pourraient expliquer la satisfaction, et les données ne permettent pas d'isoler l'effet du comité. Ils ne le rejettent pas pour autant comme une erreur.
4. D — Criteria are written down but rarely decisive.. 43 % des acheteurs intègrent formellement ces critères, mais seuls 12 % disent qu'ils ont été décisifs : l'écart entre la règle affichée et la pratique reste large. Rien ne dit que les acheteurs ignorent volontairement les règles.

Exercice 4 — C1-M3-L3-I4 (C2, C1.1)

Complétez la note méthodologique avec le terme qui convient.

The survey was completed by 2,100 [1] _____, weighted by region and company size; the [2] _____ is approximately ±2 points. Usage data are [3] _____ and may therefore overstate actual adoption. Two [4] _____ with unusually high spending were excluded from the averages. Readers should note an important [5] _____: the total [6] _____ market is estimated, not measured, and it would be unwise to [7] _____ these results to smaller economies.

[1] correspondents / responders / respondents / answerers

[2] error margin / margin of error / error rate / margin of mistake

[3] self-reported / self-made / self-evident / self-assessed

[4] outputs / outsiders / outcomes / outliers

[5] clause / cavity / caveat / disclaimer

[6] adjustable / addressable / accessible / attainable

[7] extrapolate / exaggerate / extract / expand

Corrigé

[1] respondents. « respondents » = personnes ayant répondu à une enquête. « correspondents » désigne des journalistes ou des personnes avec qui l'on correspond.
[2] margin of error. L'expression consacrée est « margin of error ». « error rate » est un taux d'erreurs (par exemple de saisie), notion différente.
[3] self-reported. « self-reported » = déclaré par les intéressés, d'où le risque de surestimation. « self-evident » signifie « évident ».
[4] outliers. « outliers » = valeurs aberrantes exclues des moyennes. « outsiders » désigne des personnes extérieures à un groupe.
[5] caveat. « caveat » = réserve, mise en garde sur l'interprétation. « disclaimer » est une clause de non-responsabilité, plus juridique.
[6] addressable. « addressable market » = marché adressable, terme consacré en analyse de marché. « accessible market » n'est pas l'expression d'usage.
[7] extrapolate. « to extrapolate to » = généraliser des résultats à une autre population. « extract » signifie extraire.

title: C1-M3 — Clauses contractuelles et conditions générales : l'anglais juridique des affaires
description: Interpréter correctement la valeur de shall, may, must, will et des marqueurs subject to, provided that, notwithstanding et unless dans une clause de 300 à 450 mots. Identifier dans des conditions générales qui supporte une obligation, un risque ou un coût, et dans quelles conditions, avec au moins 75 % de réponses correctes. Reformuler en français simple le sens d'au moins cinq termes juridiques courants (indemnify, force majeure, liquidated damages, terminate for convenience, governing law).

sections.title: C1-M3-L4 — Clauses contractuelles et conditions générales : l'anglais juridique des affaires
sections.contentHtml:
Objectifs :

  • Interpréter correctement la valeur de shall, may, must, will et des marqueurs subject to, provided that, notwithstanding et unless dans une clause de 300 à 450 mots.
  • Identifier dans des conditions générales qui supporte une obligation, un risque ou un coût, et dans quelles conditions, avec au moins 75 % de réponses correctes.
  • Reformuler en français simple le sens d'au moins cinq termes juridiques courants (indemnify, force majeure, liquidated damages, terminate for convenience, governing law).

Compétence C2 — niveau C1.2 — 40 min

Cette leçon est un entraînement linguistique : elle vous apprend à comprendre la langue des contrats rédigés en anglais, pas à les interpréter juridiquement. Pour toute décision, l'avis d'un juriste reste indispensable.

1. Les verbes de modalité. Dans un contrat :

  • shall exprime une obligation (The Supplier shall deliver… = le fournisseur doit livrer) ;
  • may exprime une faculté (The Buyer may terminate… = l'acheteur peut résilier, s'il le souhaite) ;
  • shall not exprime une interdiction ;
  • will est souvent utilisé comme shall dans les contrats modernes, plus lisibles.

Confondre may et shall est l'erreur la plus coûteuse : une faculté n'est pas un engagement.

2. Les marqueurs qui conditionnent ou écartent.

  • subject to clause 9 = sous réserve de la clause 9 (la clause 9 l'emporte) ;
  • notwithstanding clause 9 = nonobstant la clause 9 (cette clause-ci l'emporte) ;
  • provided that = à condition que ;
  • unless otherwise agreed in writing = sauf accord écrit contraire ;
  • in the event of / where = en cas de / lorsque.

Les questions de compréhension portent très souvent sur ce qui prime ou sur la condition d'une obligation.

3. Les clauses classiques.

  • Liquidated damages : pénalités forfaitaires convenues d'avance (par exemple pour retard), souvent plafonnées (capped at).
  • Force majeure : événement imprévisible et extérieur qui suspend les obligations ; la clause précise souvent un délai de notification et une durée au-delà de laquelle on peut résilier.
  • Limitation of liability : plafond de responsabilité, avec des exclusions (indirect or consequential loss, loss of profit).
  • Indemnify : garantir, indemniser l'autre partie contre certaines réclamations de tiers.
  • Terminate for cause / for convenience : résilier pour manquement / sans motif, moyennant préavis.
  • Automatic renewal : reconduction tacite, sauf préavis (notice of non-renewal).
  • Governing law and jurisdiction : droit applicable et tribunaux compétents.

4. Les tournures caractéristiques. Hereinafter referred to as (ci-après dénommé), the foregoing (ce qui précède), in no event shall (en aucun cas), to the extent permitted by law (dans la mesure permise par la loi), time is of the essence (les délais sont impératifs). Les phrases sont longues : repérez le sujet, le verbe modal et les conditions, puis reconstruisez la phrase.

5. Lire l'implicite d'un contrat. Ce qui manque compte : une clause de responsabilité qui exclut le « loss of data » sans prévoir de sauvegarde, ou un renouvellement automatique avec préavis de 90 jours, crée un risque pour le client. Dans un courriel de juriste interne, le ton (I would strongly recommend, I am not comfortable with) indique le degré d'alerte.

Méthode : pour chaque question, identifiez la clause concernée, puis vérifiez le modal (shall/may), la condition (provided that, unless) et l'exception (save that, except). Les distracteurs transforment fréquemment une faculté en obligation ou oublient une exception.

Langue clé

AnglaisFrançaisUsage
The Supplier shall deliver the Goods within 30 days.Le Fournisseur livre (doit livrer) les Marchandises sous 30 jours.shall = obligation contractuelle
The Customer may terminate this Agreement on 60 days' notice.Le Client peut résilier le présent Contrat moyennant un préavis de 60 jours.may = faculté, non obligation
Subject to clause 12, the Supplier's liability is limited to…Sous réserve de la clause 12, la responsabilité du Fournisseur est limitée à…la clause 12 prime sur la présente
Notwithstanding the foregoing, …Nonobstant ce qui précède, …introduit une exception qui l'emporte
In no event shall either party be liable for indirect loss.En aucun cas l'une ou l'autre partie ne sera responsable des préjudices indirects.exclusion de responsabilité
Unless either party gives notice of non-renewal at least 90 days before…Sauf si l'une des parties notifie son refus de reconduction au moins 90 jours avant…condition d'une reconduction tacite

Vocabulaire

TermeTraductionExemple
liquidated damagespénalités forfaitaires (dommages-intérêts fixés d'avance)Liquidated damages shall be capped at 10% of the order value.
force majeureforce majeureNeither party shall be liable for delays caused by force majeure.
to indemnifygarantir, indemniserThe Supplier shall indemnify the Buyer against third-party claims.
to terminate for conveniencerésilier sans motifThe Buyer may terminate for convenience on 90 days' notice.
material breachmanquement graveEither party may terminate in the event of a material breach.
governing lawdroit applicableThis Agreement is governed by the laws of Ireland.
notwithstandingnonobstant, malgréNotwithstanding clause 7, payment remains due.
subject tosous réserve deSubject to availability, orders will ship within 48 hours.
provided thatà condition queReturns are accepted provided that the goods are unused.
consequential losspréjudice indirectConsequential loss, including loss of profit, is excluded.
to waiverenoncer à (un droit)Failure to enforce a right shall not be deemed to waive it.
automatic renewalreconduction taciteThe subscription is subject to automatic renewal.
hereinafterci-aprèsTessaly Energy Ltd (hereinafter “the Client”)…
time is of the essencele respect des délais est une condition essentielleTime is of the essence for all delivery dates.

Dialogue : Relire un contrat fournisseur avec la juriste interne

Bureau d'une PME d'équipements énergétiques à Dublin. Un responsable commercial relit avec la juriste interne un projet de contrat d'approvisionnement avant signature.

PersonnageRépliqueTraduction
Conor FitzgeraldNadia, the client wants to sign by Friday. Is there anything that worries you?Nadia, le client veut signer d'ici vendredi. Y a-t-il quelque chose qui t'inquiète ?
Nadia RahimiA couple of things. Start with clause 8. It says we 'shall' deliver within six weeks, and time is of the essence.Deux ou trois choses. Commençons par la clause 8. Elle dit que nous « devons » livrer sous six semaines, et que les délais sont impératifs.
Conor FitzgeraldSix weeks is fine. We usually manage five.Six semaines, ça va. Nous livrons généralement en cinq.
Nadia RahimiUsually. But with 'time is of the essence', one late delivery could let them terminate the whole contract.Généralement. Mais avec cette mention, une seule livraison en retard pourrait leur permettre de résilier tout le contrat.
Conor FitzgeraldThat seems harsh. What about the penalties?Ça paraît sévère. Et les pénalités ?
Nadia RahimiLiquidated damages at one per cent per week, which is standard. The problem is that there's no cap.Des pénalités forfaitaires de un pour cent par semaine, c'est classique. Le problème, c'est qu'il n'y a pas de plafond.
Conor FitzgeraldSo in theory they could exceed the value of the order?Donc en théorie, elles pourraient dépasser la valeur de la commande ?
Nadia RahimiIn theory, yes. I'd ask for a cap at ten per cent and remove the 'time is of the essence' wording.En théorie, oui. Je demanderais un plafond à dix pour cent et la suppression de la mention sur les délais impératifs.
Conor FitzgeraldAnd the force majeure clause? Last year's port strike cost us a month.Et la clause de force majeure ? La grève portuaire de l'an dernier nous a coûté un mois.
Nadia RahimiTheir draft only covers natural disasters and war. Strikes at third-party facilities aren't included.Leur projet ne couvre que les catastrophes naturelles et la guerre. Les grèves dans des installations tierces n'y figurent pas.
Conor FitzgeraldSo a strike like that wouldn't excuse a delay.Donc une grève de ce type n'excuserait pas un retard.
Nadia RahimiAs drafted, no. That's the clause I'm least comfortable with.Telle que rédigée, non. C'est la clause qui me met le plus mal à l'aise.
Conor FitzgeraldFine. Can you put the three points in an email I can forward to them?D'accord. Peux-tu mettre les trois points dans un mail que je pourrai leur transférer ?
Nadia RahimiOf course. And remember, Friday is their deadline, not ours. It's worth taking two more days to get this right.Bien sûr. Et n'oublie pas : vendredi, c'est leur échéance, pas la nôtre. Cela vaut la peine de prendre deux jours de plus pour bien faire.

Exercices corrigés

Exercice 1 — C1-M3-L4-I1 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez l'extrait de contrat d'approvisionnement et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte. (Entraînement linguistique, pas d'analyse juridique.)

SUPPLY AGREEMENT — EXTRACT
between Brackwater Components Ltd (hereinafter “the Supplier”) and Tessaly Energy Ltd (hereinafter “the Buyer”)

  1. Delivery

7.1 The Supplier shall deliver the Goods to the Buyer's site in Cork within forty-two (42) days of the date of each Purchase Order, unless a later date is specified in that Purchase Order.
7.2 The Supplier shall notify the Buyer in writing without delay if it becomes aware of any circumstance likely to delay delivery, stating the cause and the expected new delivery date. Such notification shall not relieve the Supplier of its obligations under clause 7.3.
7.3 If the Supplier fails to deliver by the date determined under clause 7.1, it shall pay to the Buyer, as liquidated damages and not as a penalty, an amount equal to one per cent (1%) of the price of the delayed Goods for each complete week of delay, up to a maximum of ten per cent (10%) of that price.
7.4 Payment of liquidated damages under clause 7.3 shall be the Buyer's sole financial remedy for late delivery, save that the Buyer may terminate the relevant Purchase Order by written notice if the delay exceeds eight (8) weeks.

  1. Force Majeure

8.1 Neither party shall be liable for any failure or delay in performing its obligations to the extent that such failure or delay results from events beyond its reasonable control, including natural disasters, epidemics, acts of government, war, and strikes or other industrial action, provided that industrial action involving the affected party's own employees shall not constitute force majeure.
8.2 The affected party shall notify the other party within five (5) business days of becoming aware of the force majeure event and shall use reasonable endeavours to mitigate its effects.
8.3 If a force majeure event prevents performance for a continuous period of more than ninety (90) days, either party may terminate this Agreement with immediate effect by written notice.

  1. Limitation of Liability

9.1 Subject to clause 9.2, the Supplier's total liability arising under or in connection with this Agreement in any calendar year shall not exceed the total price paid by the Buyer in that year.
9.2 Nothing in this Agreement shall limit or exclude either party's liability for death or personal injury caused by its negligence, or for fraud.
9.3 In no event shall either party be liable for any loss of profit or any indirect or consequential loss.

1. According to clause 7.2, what happens if the Supplier informs the Buyer in advance of a likely delay?
A. The delivery date is automatically postponed to the new date stated in the Supplier's notification.
B. The Supplier is no longer required to pay liquidated damages.
C. The Buyer must accept the new delivery date.
D. The Supplier still owes liquidated damages if late.

2. If a delivery is twelve weeks late, which of the following is correct under clauses 7.3 and 7.4?
A. The Buyer may claim 12% of the price of the delayed Goods.
B. The Buyer may claim 10% and may cancel that Purchase Order.
C. The Buyer may claim unlimited damages, including compensation for any profit lost because of the delay.
D. The Buyer must terminate the whole Agreement.

3. Under clause 8.1, a strike by the Supplier's own workforce
A. is treated as force majeure in the same way as a natural disaster.
B. allows the Supplier to terminate the Agreement immediately.
C. does not count as force majeure for the Supplier.
D. must be notified within ninety days.

4. What does “use reasonable endeavours to mitigate its effects” require of the affected party?
A. To make sensible efforts to limit the consequences of the event.
B. To guarantee that the event will have no consequences.
C. To pay compensation for all the effects of the event.
D. To wait until the event has ended before acting.

5. How does clause 9.2 relate to clause 9.1?
A. It confirms that the annual cap applies to all types of liability.
B. It sets out cases to which the annual cap does not apply.
C. It increases the cap to twice the annual price.
D. It applies only to the Buyer.

Corrigé

1. D — The Supplier still owes liquidated damages if late.. « Such notification shall not relieve the Supplier of its obligations under clause 7.3 » : prévenir ne dispense pas des pénalités de retard. Le piège est de croire qu'une notification déplace l'échéance ; le texte ne le prévoit nulle part.
2. B — The Buyer may claim 10% and may cancel that Purchase Order.. Les pénalités sont de 1 % par semaine mais plafonnées à 10 % (« up to a maximum of ten per cent »), et au-delà de 8 semaines l'acheteur « may terminate the relevant Purchase Order ». « may » = faculté, pas obligation ; et seule la commande concernée est visée, pas tout le contrat.
3. C — does not count as force majeure for the Supplier.. La clause inclut les grèves mais avec une exception introduite par « provided that » : la grève du propre personnel de la partie concernée « shall not constitute force majeure ». Le délai de notification est de 5 jours ouvrés, 90 jours étant la durée ouvrant droit à résiliation.
4. A — To make sensible efforts to limit the consequences of the event.. « reasonable endeavours » = des efforts raisonnables, une obligation de moyens ; « mitigate » = atténuer. Il ne s'agit ni d'une garantie de résultat ni d'une indemnisation.
5. B — It sets out cases to which the annual cap does not apply.. 9.1 commence par « Subject to clause 9.2 » : la clause 9.2 prime et exclut du plafond la responsabilité pour décès, dommages corporels dus à une négligence et fraude. Elle vise « either party », pas seulement l'acheteur.

Exercice 2 — C1-M3-L4-I2 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez l'extrait des conditions générales d'un service en ligne et répondez aux questions. (Entraînement linguistique, pas de conseil juridique.)

LUMENDESK — TERMS OF SERVICE FOR BUSINESS CUSTOMERS (EXTRACT)

  1. Subscription Term and Renewal

4.1 Each subscription begins on the Start Date shown in the Order Form and continues for an initial term of twelve (12) months.
4.2 Thereafter, the subscription shall renew automatically for successive periods of twelve (12) months unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal at least ninety (90) days before the end of the current term.
4.3 Lumendesk may revise its fees with effect from any renewal date by giving the Customer at least sixty (60) days' prior notice. If the Customer does not accept the revised fees, its sole remedy shall be to give notice of non-renewal in accordance with clause 4.2.

  1. Customer Data

5.1 As between the parties, the Customer retains all rights in the data it uploads to the Service (“Customer Data”).
5.2 Lumendesk shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect Customer Data. The Customer acknowledges, however, that it remains responsible for maintaining independent back-up copies of any Customer Data it considers critical.
5.3 Upon termination, the Customer may export its Customer Data for a period of thirty (30) days. Thereafter, Lumendesk shall be entitled to delete all Customer Data without further notice.

  1. Service Levels

6.1 Lumendesk will use commercially reasonable efforts to make the Service available 99.5% of the time in each calendar month, excluding scheduled maintenance.
6.2 If availability falls below that level, the Customer shall be entitled to a service credit as set out in Schedule 2, provided that it submits a claim within fifteen (15) days of the end of the month concerned. Service credits constitute the Customer's sole and exclusive remedy for any failure to meet the availability target.

  1. Liability

7.1 To the extent permitted by law, Lumendesk's aggregate liability under these Terms shall not exceed the fees paid by the Customer in the six (6) months preceding the event giving rise to the claim.
7.2 Lumendesk shall not be liable for any loss or corruption of data, loss of profit, or indirect or consequential loss, howsoever arising.

1. A customer whose initial term ends on 31 December wants to stop the service. What must it do?
A. Simply stop paying after 31 December.
B. Send a written notice of termination at any time before the end of December, when the term expires.
C. Send written notice of non-renewal no later than about the beginning of October.
D. Wait for Lumendesk to propose new fees.

2. What can the customer do if it disagrees with a fee increase?
A. Refuse the revised fees and continue using the service at the old price until the end of the term.
B. Terminate immediately and claim a refund.
C. Ask for a service credit.
D. Give notice of non-renewal (clause 4.2).

3. Read together, what do clauses 5.2 and 7.2 imply for the customer?
A. It bears the risk of data loss and should keep its own back-ups.
B. Lumendesk will compensate it fully for any lost data.
C. It loses ownership of its data when it uploads it.
D. It can recover deleted data at any time after termination.

4. In clause 6.1, what does “will use commercially reasonable efforts” suggest about the 99.5% availability figure?
A. It is a firm guarantee whose breach allows termination.
B. It is a target rather than an absolute promise.
C. It includes periods of scheduled maintenance.
D. It applies only during the initial term.

Corrigé

1. C — Send written notice of non-renewal no later than about the beginning of October.. La reconduction est automatique « unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal at least ninety (90) days before the end of the current term » : pour un terme au 31 décembre, le préavis doit partir début octobre au plus tard. Un préavis en décembre serait trop tardif.
2. D — Give notice of non-renewal (clause 4.2).. « its sole remedy shall be to give notice of non-renewal » : le seul recours est de ne pas renouveler. « sole remedy » exclut le maintien de l'ancien prix ou un remboursement.
3. A — It bears the risk of data loss and should keep its own back-ups.. 5.2 met les sauvegardes à la charge du client et 7.2 exclut la responsabilité de Lumendesk pour « loss or corruption of data » : le risque pèse sur le client. 5.1 confirme qu'il reste titulaire de ses données ; l'export n'est possible que 30 jours après la résiliation.
4. B — It is a target rather than an absolute promise.. « commercially reasonable efforts » marque une obligation de moyens : 99,5 % est un objectif, et le seul recours en cas de manquement est l'avoir (« sole and exclusive remedy »). La maintenance programmée est explicitement exclue du calcul.

Exercice 3 — C1-M3-L4-I3 (C2, C1.1)

Lisez le courriel de la juriste interne et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

From: Nadia Rahimi <n.rahimi@tessaly-energy.example>
To: Conor Fitzgerald <c.fitzgerald@tessaly-energy.example>
Subject: RE: Halden Grid contract — comments before signature

Conor,

Thanks for sending over the latest draft. I appreciate that Halden Grid is keen to sign by Friday, and I do not want to hold things up unnecessarily. Most of the document is in good shape, and the commercial terms you negotiated look sensible. There are, however, three points I would not be comfortable signing as they stand.

First, clause 8.4 states that “time is of the essence” for every delivery date. In practice, this would allow Halden to terminate the entire agreement after a single late delivery, however minor. Given our recent experience with port congestion, I would strongly recommend deleting this wording. Their procurement team has accepted similar changes from other suppliers, so I don't expect much resistance.

Second, the liquidated damages in clause 9 are set at 1% per week with no upper limit. The rate itself is market standard, but the absence of a cap is not. I suggest proposing a cap of 10% of the value of the delayed order, which is what we agreed with our two largest customers last year.

Third — and this is the one that concerns me most — the force majeure clause covers natural disasters, epidemics and war but makes no mention of strikes or disruption at third-party facilities such as ports or rail terminals. As you know, it was precisely this kind of event that delayed the Bremen order last spring. If we accept the clause as drafted, a similar incident would leave us fully exposed to the damages in clause 9.

I have prepared marked-up wording for all three points, attached. I'd suggest you present them as a package rather than one by one; in my experience, that tends to produce a quicker agreement.

One last thought: Friday is Halden's deadline, not a contractual one. If they need two or three extra days to review our comments, that seems a small price to pay for getting the terms right.

Best,
Nadia

1. What is Nadia's overall attitude to the draft contract?
A. Generally satisfied but unwilling to accept certain clauses without changes.
B. Strongly opposed to signing it under any circumstances.
C. Entirely satisfied, provided it is signed by Friday.
D. Indifferent to the details, since the commercial terms negotiated by Conor are not her responsibility.

2. Why does Nadia expect Halden Grid to accept the change to clause 8.4?
A. Because the clause is illegal in Ireland.
B. Because Halden has agreed to similar requests from other suppliers.
C. Because Halden itself proposed deleting it.
D. Because port congestion has now ended.

3. Which of the three points worries Nadia most, and why?
A. The rate of liquidated damages, because it is far above market standard.
B. The “time is of the essence” wording, because it would allow Halden to terminate the agreement after any single late delivery.
C. The proposed 10% cap, because it is too low for Halden.
D. The force majeure clause, as it omits third-party disruption.

4. What does Nadia imply in her final paragraph?
A. The contract becomes void if it is not signed by Friday.
B. Conor should sign the contract on Friday as planned and negotiate the three changes afterwards.
C. A short delay is worth it for better terms.
D. Halden will certainly refuse to wait.

Corrigé

1. A — Generally satisfied but unwilling to accept certain clauses without changes.. « Most of the document is in good shape… There are, however, three points I would not be comfortable signing as they stand » : satisfaction globale avec des réserves ciblées. « as they stand » montre qu'elle accepterait le contrat une fois modifié.
2. B — Because Halden has agreed to similar requests from other suppliers.. « Their procurement team has accepted similar changes from other suppliers, so I don't expect much resistance. » Rien n'indique que la clause soit illégale ; la congestion portuaire est au contraire un risque actuel.
3. D — The force majeure clause, as it omits third-party disruption.. « this is the one that concerns me most » introduit la clause de force majeure, qui ne couvre pas les perturbations dans les ports ou terminaux. Le taux de 1 % est jugé « market standard » : c'est l'absence de plafond qui pose problème.
4. C — A short delay is worth it for better terms.. « Friday is Halden's deadline, not a contractual one… a small price to pay » : quelques jours de retard valent mieux que de mauvaises conditions. Elle ne suggère jamais de signer d'abord pour négocier ensuite.

Exercice 4 — C1-M3-L4-I4 (C2, C1.2)

Complétez la clause avec le terme qui convient dans chaque liste.

[1] _____ clause 11, the Supplier [2] _____ indemnify the Customer against any third-party claim alleging that the Software infringes intellectual property rights, [3] _____ the Customer notifies the Supplier of the claim within ten days. [4] _____ shall the Supplier be liable for consequential loss. The Customer [5] _____ terminate this Agreement for convenience on ninety days' written notice. Failure to enforce any provision shall not be deemed a [6] _____ of that provision.

[1] Owing to / Subjected to / Due to / Subject to

[2] may / might / shall / would

[3] unless / provided that / whereas / so that

[4] In no event / At any event / In any case / On no account of

[5] shall / must / is to / may

[6] warrant / waver / waiver / wager

Corrigé

[1] Subject to. « Subject to clause 11 » = sous réserve de la clause 11, qui prime. « Due to » / « Owing to » expriment une cause et changeraient le sens.
[2] shall. L'indemnisation est une obligation du fournisseur : « shall ». « may » en ferait une simple faculté, ce qui viderait la garantie de son sens.
[3] provided that. « provided that » = à condition que : la garantie dépend d'une notification sous dix jours. « unless » inverserait la condition.
[4] In no event. « In no event shall… » = en aucun cas, avec inversion sujet-verbe. « In any case » ne permet pas l'inversion et n'exprime pas l'exclusion.
[5] may. La résiliation sans motif est une faculté offerte au client : « may ». « shall » ou « must » l'obligeraient à résilier.
[6] waiver. « waiver » = renonciation à un droit. « waver » (hésiter) est un paronyme fréquent ; « warrant » signifie garantir.

title: C1-M3 — Politiques internes : ESG, conformité et lancement d'alerte
description: Repérer dans une politique interne de 350 à 450 mots le champ d'application, les obligations, les seuils et les exceptions. Distinguer le degré de contrainte exprimé par must, are required to, should, are expected to et are encouraged to. Évaluer la précision d'un engagement ESG (cible chiffrée, échéance, périmètre) et repérer au moins deux formulations vagues, avec au moins 75 % de réponses correctes aux QCM.
