sections.title: Quiz de validation du module (corrigé)
sections.contentHtml:
Seuil de réussite : 70 %.

Exercice 1 — C1-M3-Q1 (C2, C1.1)

Lisez l'extrait de rapport annuel et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

Chair's Letter — Aldwych Hospitality Group plc, Annual Report 2025

Dear Shareholders,

When I wrote to you a year ago, I described 2024 as a year of stabilisation. I am pleased to report that 2025 has been a year of genuine progress. Group revenue rose by 9% to £1.14 billion, occupancy across our 86 hotels averaged 78%, and adjusted earnings per share returned to the level last seen before the pandemic. Our net debt, which peaked at more than four times earnings in 2022, now stands at 2.3 times, comfortably within the target range set by the Board.

These results did not happen by chance. They reflect difficult decisions taken over the past three years, including the sale of eleven hotels that no longer fitted our strategy and a significant reduction in head office costs. Not all of these decisions were popular, and I am grateful to colleagues and shareholders who supported them when the outcome was far from certain.

It would, however, be premature to declare victory. Wage costs rose by 7% during the year, ahead of the growth in room rates, and we expect this pressure to persist as the labour market remains tight. Demand from corporate travellers, historically our most profitable segment, has recovered to only 85% of its 2019 level, and we no longer assume that it will return in full. Our plans are built accordingly.

In light of the improvement in our financial position, the Board is recommending a final dividend of 6.5 pence per share, the first full-year dividend since 2019. We intend to pursue a progressive dividend policy from here, while retaining the flexibility to invest in the refurbishment of our older properties, several of which are now falling behind the expectations of today's guests.

Finally, after eight years as Chair, I have informed the Board that I will not seek re-election at next year's Annual General Meeting. The search for my successor is well advanced, and I am confident that the Group will be in good hands.

Eleanor Whitcombe
Chair

1. How does the Chair compare 2025 with the previous year?
A. 2025 was simply a continuation of the stabilisation seen in 2024.
B. 2025 was disappointing compared with 2024.
C. 2025 showed real improvement after a year of stabilisation.
D. 2025 was the first year in which the Group made a profit.

2. What does the Chair imply about the decisions taken over the past three years?
A. They were risky and contested at the time, but have been vindicated.
B. They were unanimously supported from the start.
C. They have not yet produced any measurable improvement in the Group's results.
D. They will need to be reversed in 2026.

3. What is the Chair's attitude to corporate travel demand?
A. She expects it to recover strongly and to exceed its 2019 level as early as next year.
B. She believes it has fully recovered.
C. She considers it irrelevant to the Group's profitability.
D. She accepts it may never fully recover.

Corrigé

1. C — 2025 showed real improvement after a year of stabilisation.. « a year of stabilisation » (2024) s'oppose à « a year of genuine progress » (2025). Rien n'indique que le groupe faisait des pertes auparavant ; le BPA « returned to » un niveau antérieur.
2. A — They were risky and contested at the time, but have been vindicated.. « Not all of these decisions were popular » et le soutien reçu « when the outcome was far from certain » suggèrent des décisions contestées, désormais justifiées par les résultats. L'unanimité est donc exclue.
3. D — She accepts it may never fully recover.. « we no longer assume that it will return in full. Our plans are built accordingly » : attitude réaliste et prudente. Elle rappelle au contraire que c'est historiquement le segment le plus rentable.

Exercice 2 — C1-M3-Q2 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez cette tribune et répondez aux questions dans l'ordre du texte.

Let algorithms help with hiring — but not decide it
by Dr Naomi Ferreira, organisational psychologist

It has become fashionable in some boardrooms to describe artificial intelligence as the cure for everything that is wrong with recruitment. Human recruiters, the argument goes, are slow, inconsistent and riddled with unconscious bias; software, by contrast, can screen thousands of applications in minutes and judge every candidate by the same criteria. Vendors have been quick to promise “bias-free hiring” at the click of a button.

I have some sympathy with the diagnosis. Anyone who has studied traditional interviews knows how easily they are swayed by a confident handshake, a shared university or a familiar accent. If technology can reduce the influence of such factors, it deserves a hearing.

The trouble is that the cure can replicate the disease. An algorithm trained on a company's past hiring decisions will learn the preferences embedded in those decisions, including the ones nobody would defend openly. If a firm has historically promoted people who look and sound like its founders, a system that learns from that history will, quite logically, conclude that this is what success looks like. The bias does not disappear; it simply becomes harder to see, because it now carries the authority of mathematics.

There is also a question of accountability. When a human manager rejects a candidate, someone can be asked to explain the decision. When a model does so, the answer is too often a shrug: the system is proprietary, the weights are complex, the vendor cannot say. That is not good enough for decisions that shape people's livelihoods.

None of this is an argument for abandoning the technology. Used to widen the pool of candidates, to anonymise applications or to flag inconsistencies in interviewers' scoring, it can make hiring fairer. But the final decision must remain with people who can be held to account — and companies should be required to test their tools regularly for discriminatory outcomes and to publish the results. Efficiency is a worthy goal. It is not the only one.

1. How does the writer present the idea that AI is “the cure for everything that is wrong with recruitment”?
A. As her own firm conviction.
B. As a scientifically proven fact.
C. As a view held by others, which she regards with some distance.
D. As a claim made only by job candidates.

2. What does the writer mean by “the cure can replicate the disease”?
A. Algorithms may reproduce existing biases.
B. AI tools are too expensive for most companies.
C. Recruiters will lose their jobs because of AI.
D. Software is not yet able to process the large numbers of applications that firms receive.

3. What is the writer's overall position?
A. AI should replace human recruiters entirely, since they are slow and inconsistent.
B. AI should be banned from recruitment.
C. Vendors' promises are fully justified.
D. AI can make hiring fairer if people keep the final say and tools are tested.

Corrigé

1. C — As a view held by others, which she regards with some distance.. « It has become fashionable… », « the argument goes », « Vendors have been quick to promise » : l'idée est attribuée à d'autres (dirigeants, éditeurs), avec une distance ironique. Ce n'est pas son opinion.
2. A — Algorithms may reproduce existing biases.. Le paragraphe explique qu'un algorithme entraîné sur des décisions passées « will learn the preferences embedded in those decisions » : le remède reproduit le mal (les biais). Le coût et l'emploi ne sont pas évoqués.
3. D — AI can make hiring fairer if people keep the final say and tools are tested.. « None of this is an argument for abandoning the technology… But the final decision must remain with people » + tests réguliers publiés : position nuancée, ni rejet ni adhésion totale.

Exercice 3 — C1-M3-Q3 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez l'extrait de contrat de prestation et répondez aux questions. (Entraînement linguistique, pas de conseil juridique.)

CONSULTANCY SERVICES AGREEMENT — EXTRACT
between Orrin Advisory Ltd (“the Consultant”) and Vantrell Medical Devices plc (“the Client”)

  1. Confidentiality

11.1 Each party shall keep confidential all information of a confidential nature disclosed to it by the other party in connection with this Agreement (“Confidential Information”) and shall not use such information except for the purpose of performing its obligations under this Agreement.
11.2 Clause 11.1 shall not apply to information which (a) is or becomes publicly available other than through a breach of this Agreement; (b) was lawfully in the receiving party's possession before disclosure; or (c) is required to be disclosed by law or by any regulatory authority, provided that, where permitted, the receiving party gives the disclosing party prompt written notice of such requirement.
11.3 The obligations in this clause 11 shall survive termination of this Agreement for a period of five (5) years.

  1. Non-solicitation

12.1 During the term of this Agreement and for twelve (12) months after its termination, the Client shall not, without the prior written consent of the Consultant, directly or indirectly solicit or employ any individual who has been engaged by the Consultant in the provision of the Services.
12.2 Clause 12.1 shall not prevent the Client from employing any individual who responds to a general advertisement not specifically directed at the Consultant's personnel.
12.3 If the Client breaches clause 12.1, it shall pay the Consultant, by way of compensation, a sum equal to thirty per cent (30%) of the individual's annual gross salary in their new position.

  1. Termination

13.1 Either party may terminate this Agreement by giving not less than sixty (60) days' written notice to the other.
13.2 Notwithstanding clause 13.1, either party may terminate this Agreement with immediate effect by written notice if the other party commits a material breach which, being capable of remedy, has not been remedied within twenty-one (21) days of a written request to do so.
13.3 On termination for any reason, the Client shall pay all fees properly incurred up to the date of termination.

  1. Governing Law

This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of England and Wales.

1. Under clause 11.2(c), if a regulator requires the Consultant to disclose Confidential Information, the Consultant
A. must refuse to disclose it in all circumstances.
B. may disclose it, telling the Client if allowed.
C. must first obtain the Client's written consent.
D. is released from all its confidentiality obligations towards the Client for five years.

2. Six months after the end of the Agreement, the Client hires a consultant from Orrin who applied in response to a public job advertisement. According to clause 12,
A. the Client must pay 30% of the person's annual salary.
B. the Client must obtain Orrin's prior written consent, as the 12-month period has not ended.
C. the hiring is prohibited for five years.
D. the hiring is permitted because of the exception in clause 12.2.

3. What is the relationship between clauses 13.1 and 13.2?
A. 13.2 permits immediate termination in specific cases, overriding the notice in 13.1.
B. 13.2 cancels the right to terminate on notice.
C. 13.1 applies only to the Client and 13.2 only to the Consultant.
D. 13.2 requires the terminating party to give 21 days' written notice in every case of termination.

Corrigé

1. B — may disclose it, telling the Client if allowed.. La divulgation exigée par une autorité est une exception, « provided that, where permitted, the receiving party gives… prompt written notice » : il faut informer, pas obtenir un accord. Les autres obligations demeurent.
2. D — the hiring is permitted because of the exception in clause 12.2.. 12.2 exclut du champ de l'interdiction les recrutements issus d'une « general advertisement not specifically directed at the Consultant's personnel ». La compensation de 30 % ne s'applique qu'en cas de violation de 12.1.
3. A — 13.2 permits immediate termination in specific cases, overriding the notice in 13.1.. « Notwithstanding clause 13.1 » : la clause 13.2 l'emporte pour un cas précis (manquement grave non corrigé sous 21 jours). Le délai de 21 jours est celui laissé pour remédier au manquement, pas un préavis général.

Exercice 4 — C1-M3-Q4 (C2, C1.1)

Lisez l'extrait du code de conduite fournisseurs et répondez aux questions.

BRIGHTWATER HOME STORES — SUPPLIER CODE OF CONDUCT (EXTRACT), Edition 2026

  1. Application

This Code applies to all suppliers of goods and services to Brightwater Home Stores and its subsidiaries. Suppliers are responsible for ensuring that their own subcontractors and sub-suppliers involved in the production of goods for Brightwater comply with standards equivalent to those set out below. Brightwater recognises that the depth of visibility suppliers have over their supply chains varies, and expects continuous improvement rather than immediate perfection beyond the first tier.

  1. Labour standards

Suppliers must not use forced, bonded or child labour in any form. Workers must be free to leave their employment on reasonable notice, and suppliers must not retain identity documents or require workers to pay recruitment fees. Working hours must comply with national law and, in any case, must not exceed 60 hours per week, including overtime, except in exceptional circumstances agreed in advance with Brightwater. Suppliers should pay wages that meet at least the legal minimum and are encouraged to work towards a living wage.

  1. Environment

Suppliers must comply with all applicable environmental laws. Suppliers whose annual sales to Brightwater exceed £2 million are required to report their Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions annually from 2027 and to set a reduction target by 2028. Other suppliers are encouraged to do so.

  1. Monitoring and remediation

Brightwater may carry out announced or unannounced audits of supplier sites, either directly or through independent auditors. Where non-compliance is identified, Brightwater will normally work with the supplier on a corrective action plan with agreed deadlines. Termination of the business relationship will generally be considered only where a supplier refuses to engage or fails repeatedly to implement agreed actions. However, any evidence of forced or child labour will result in immediate suspension of orders pending investigation.

  1. Reporting concerns

Workers and other stakeholders may report concerns confidentially through Brightwater's independent ethics line, available in 14 languages.

1. What does section 1 suggest about Brightwater's expectations regarding sub-suppliers?
A. Brightwater audits every sub-supplier itself.
B. Sub-suppliers are entirely outside the scope of the Code.
C. Brightwater accepts that control over deeper tiers will improve gradually.
D. Suppliers must guarantee immediate and full compliance at every tier of their supply chain.

2. Which statement about wages is accurate?
A. Paying a living wage is compulsory for all suppliers.
B. Paying a living wage is recommended, while the legal minimum is expected.
C. Wages are not covered by the Code.
D. Suppliers must pay a living wage from 2027.

3. How does section 4 describe Brightwater's response to non-compliance?
A. Any non-compliance identified during an audit leads to immediate termination of the relationship.
B. Brightwater never suspends orders.
C. Audits are always announced in advance.
D. Cooperation is the norm, but forced or child labour means immediate suspension.

Corrigé

1. C — Brightwater accepts that control over deeper tiers will improve gradually.. « expects continuous improvement rather than immediate perfection beyond the first tier » : exigence progressive. Les sous-traitants ne sont pas hors champ : les fournisseurs doivent veiller à des standards équivalents.
2. B — Paying a living wage is recommended, while the legal minimum is expected.. « should pay wages that meet at least the legal minimum and are encouraged to work towards a living wage » : le salaire décent est une recommandation (« encouraged »), pas une obligation.
3. D — Cooperation is the norm, but forced or child labour means immediate suspension.. Le principe est un plan d'actions correctives ; la rupture n'intervient qu'en cas de refus ou d'échecs répétés. Exception explicite : le travail forcé ou des enfants entraîne « immediate suspension of orders ». Les audits peuvent être inopinés.

Exercice 5 — C1-M3-Q5 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez le constat d'audit et la réponse de la direction, puis répondez aux questions.

INTERNAL AUDIT — TRAVEL AND EXPENSES REVIEW, Fenmoor Engineering Ltd
Finding 2: Approval of senior management expense claims (High priority)

Observation
Under the Travel and Expenses Policy, all expense claims must be approved by the claimant's line manager before reimbursement. For members of the Executive Committee, approval is given by the Chief Executive, and the Chief Executive's own claims are approved by the Chief Financial Officer. We tested 30 claims submitted by Executive Committee members between January and June. In 11 cases, the claim had been approved by the claimant's own executive assistant using delegated system access, without evidence of review by the designated approver. In four of these cases, the claims included first-class travel, which the policy permits only with prior written authorisation; no such authorisation was on file.

Risk
Inadequate review of senior management expenses creates a risk of non-compliant or inappropriate spending and, given the seniority of the individuals involved, a reputational risk should such spending become public.

Root cause
Delegated access was set up to speed up processing while executives were travelling. The system does not distinguish between preparing a claim and approving it.

Recommendation
Remove approval rights from delegated accounts and require all Executive Committee claims to be approved personally by the designated approver. Review the four first-class claims and recover any amounts not authorised under the policy.

Management response — AGREED
We accept the finding and recommendations. Approval rights have already been removed from delegated accounts with effect from 1 September. The four first-class claims will be reviewed by the Chief Financial Officer and the Chair of the Audit Committee by 31 October, and any unauthorised amounts will be recovered. We would note that the first-class travel in question related to long-haul business trips undertaken at short notice, which we believe would have been authorised had a request been made.

1. What exactly did the auditors find in the 11 cases?
A. The claims were fraudulent.
B. The claims were approved by assistants without evidence of review by the proper approver.
C. The Chief Executive refused to approve the claims because they included first-class travel.
D. The claims had not been reimbursed.

2. According to the root cause, why did the problem arise?
A. Executives deliberately wanted to avoid controls.
B. The policy does not require any approval for executives.
C. Assistants had not been trained in the policy and did not know which claims needed approval.
D. Convenience access combined with a system that cannot separate preparing from approving.

3. What does the last sentence of the management response reveal?
A. Management agrees but plays down the first-class claims.
B. Management rejects the recommendation to review the claims.
C. Management admits that the trips were unnecessary.
D. Management confirms that written authorisation for the first-class trips had been requested in advance.

Corrigé

1. B — The claims were approved by assistants without evidence of review by the proper approver.. « approved by the claimant's own executive assistant using delegated system access, without evidence of review by the designated approver ». L'audit ne parle jamais de fraude : ce serait une lecture excessive.
2. D — Convenience access combined with a system that cannot separate preparing from approving.. L'accès délégué a été créé « to speed up processing » et le système « does not distinguish between preparing a claim and approving it ». L'audit n'attribue aucune intention délibérée aux dirigeants.
3. A — Management agrees but plays down the first-class claims.. La réponse est « AGREED », mais la dernière phrase (« which we believe would have been authorised had a request been made ») relativise la gravité : attitude légèrement défensive. Elle confirme au contraire qu'aucune demande n'a été faite.

Exercice 6 — C1-M3-Q6 (C2, C1.2)

Lisez le courriel et répondez aux questions. Attention au ton et aux sous-entendus.

From: Graham Lowther <g.lowther@kingsferry-foods.example>
To: Anya Petrova <a.petrova@cartwell-packaging.example>
Subject: Proposed price increase from 1 January

Dear Anya,

Thank you for your letter of 2 November and for taking the time to explain the reasons behind the proposed 11% increase in packaging prices from 1 January. I fully appreciate that your energy and raw material costs have risen sharply this year, and that Cartwell has absorbed a good part of those increases until now. We have always valued your reliability, particularly during last winter's disruption, when you were one of the few suppliers who delivered on time.

I must be candid with you, however. An increase of this size, at such short notice, is simply not something we are able to accept. Our own retail customers have made it very clear that they will not entertain further price rises before the spring, and an 11% increase on packaging would wipe out most of the margin we expect to make on several of our key product lines. I would also point out that, according to the published indices you referred to in your letter, the cost of board has actually fallen by around 4% since the summer.

I do not want this to become a stand-off. We would be prepared to consider an increase of up to 5% from 1 January, with a further review in April in the light of actual cost movements. We would also be open to discussing a longer-term agreement, which I imagine would give Cartwell greater security of volume.

I should mention, in the interests of transparency, that our procurement team has been asked to obtain benchmark quotations from two other suppliers as part of our normal annual review. I would much rather reach an agreement with you, but I am sure you will understand that we need to be in a position to compare.

Perhaps we could find time for a call next week?

Kind regards,

Graham Lowther
Head of Procurement, Kingsferry Foods

1. Why does Graham mention the fall in the cost of board?
A. To congratulate Cartwell on its purchasing.
B. To show that he has not read Cartwell's letter carefully.
C. To question part of the justification Cartwell gave for its increase.
D. To announce that Kingsferry will buy board directly.

2. What does Graham propose in the third paragraph?
A. To accept the full 11% increase in exchange for a longer-term supply agreement.
B. To accept a smaller increase, review it in April and possibly agree a longer-term deal.
C. To freeze prices until April.
D. To end the relationship if Cartwell refuses.

3. What is the implicit message of the fourth paragraph?
A. Kingsferry has already chosen a new supplier.
B. Kingsferry's procurement team disagrees with Graham.
C. The benchmark quotations are purely a formality and will have no consequence for Cartwell.
D. If Cartwell does not move, Kingsferry has alternatives it could turn to.

Corrigé

1. C — To question part of the justification Cartwell gave for its increase.. Il retourne contre Cartwell les indices cités dans sa propre lettre : le carton a baissé d'environ 4 %, ce qui fragilise l'argumentaire de la hausse. C'est une contestation polie (« I would also point out »).
2. B — To accept a smaller increase, review it in April and possibly agree a longer-term deal.. Jusqu'à 5 % au 1er janvier, révision en avril, et ouverture à un accord de plus long terme. Il n'accepte pas les 11 % et ne menace pas explicitement de rompre.
3. D — If Cartwell does not move, Kingsferry has alternatives it could turn to.. Présentés comme une démarche « normale », les devis de deux concurrents constituent un levier de négociation : une pression implicite. Rien n'indique qu'un autre fournisseur soit déjà choisi (« I would much rather reach an agreement with you »).

Exercice 7 — C1-M3-Q7 (C2, C1.1)

Complétez l'extrait de rapport annuel avec le terme qui convient.

Excluding a non-cash [1] _____ of £24 million, [2] _____ operating profit rose by 5%. Despite currency [3] _____, we are reiterating our full-year [4] _____, and the Board recommends a [5] _____ dividend of 12p.

[1] impairing / impediment / impairment / imprint

[2] undertaken / underlying / underlined / undergoing

[3] headwinds / headlines / headways / headcounts

[4] guidebook / guideline / guarantee / guidance

[5] closing / finishing / final / terminal

Corrigé

[1] impairment. « non-cash impairment » = dépréciation sans sortie de trésorerie. « impediment » signifie obstacle.
[2] underlying. « underlying operating profit » = résultat opérationnel retraité. « underlined » signifie souligné.
[3] headwinds. « currency headwinds » = effets de change défavorables. « headcount » désigne l'effectif.
[4] guidance. « full-year guidance » = prévisions annuelles. Une « guarantee » serait un engagement ferme, ce que les entreprises évitent.
[5] final. « final dividend » = solde du dividende annuel (par opposition à « interim dividend »).

Exercice 8 — C1-M3-Q8 (C2, C1.2)

Complétez l'extrait d'éditorial avec l'expression qui convient.

The government's new subsidy is little more than a [1] _____: it does nothing about the [2] _____, which is the chronic lack of skilled workers. Ministers clearly want to [3] _____, promising both lower taxes and higher spending. Critics [4] _____ that the plan simply [5] _____ once again.

[1] silver bullet / sticking plaster / level playing field / blank cheque

[2] elephant in the room / tip of the iceberg / light at the end of the tunnel / icing on the cake

[3] break the ice / bite the bullet / call it a day / have their cake and eat it

[4] admit / agree / argue / accept

[5] turns over a new leaf / kicks the can down the road / goes the extra mile / hits the ground running

Corrigé

[1] sticking plaster. « little more than a sticking plaster » = guère plus qu'une rustine. « silver bullet » (solution miracle) contredirait « does nothing ».
[2] elephant in the room. « the elephant in the room » = le problème évident que l'on évite. « icing on the cake » (cerise sur le gâteau) est positif.
[3] have their cake and eat it. Promettre à la fois moins d'impôts et plus de dépenses = vouloir le beurre et l'argent du beurre. « bite the bullet » signifierait accepter une décision pénible.
[4] argue. « Critics argue that… » introduit un point de vue rapporté. « admit » impliquerait une concession, illogique pour des critiques.
[5] kicks the can down the road. « kicks the can down the road » = repousse le problème. Les autres expressions sont positives et contredisent la critique.

Exercice 9 — C1-M3-Q9 (C2, C1.2)

Complétez la clause avec le terme qui convient. (Entraînement linguistique.)

[1] _____ clause 4.2, the Supplier [2] _____ deliver the Goods by the agreed date. The Buyer [3] _____ reject any Goods that do not conform, [4] _____ it notifies the Supplier within seven days. In no event shall the Supplier be liable for [5] _____ loss.

[1] Subject to / Subjected to / Owing to / Thanks to

[2] might / may / could / shall

[3] must / shall / may / is bound to

[4] unless / provided that / whereas / lest

[5] consequential / consecutive / consequent / conclusive

Corrigé

[1] Subject to. « Subject to clause 4.2 » = sous réserve de la clause 4.2. « Owing to » exprime une cause.
[2] shall. La livraison est une obligation : « shall ». « may » en ferait une simple faculté.
[3] may. Le rejet est un droit de l'acheteur, qu'il exerce s'il le souhaite : « may ».
[4] provided that. « provided that » = à condition que : le droit de rejet dépend d'une notification sous sept jours. « unless » inverserait la condition.
[5] consequential. « consequential loss » = préjudice indirect, terme consacré des clauses de responsabilité.

Exercice 10 — C1-M3-Q10 (C2, C1.1)

Complétez l'extrait de politique ESG et conformité avec le terme qui convient.

This policy applies to all staff; agents fall within its [1] _____. We will cut Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 40% against a 2023 [2] _____, without relying on [3] _____. Anyone raising a concern in good [4] _____ is protected against [5] _____.

[1] reach / range / frame / scope

[2] bottom line / baseboard / baseline / benchmark

[3] outsourcing / offsetting / outsetting / upsetting

[4] faith / belief / trust / will

[5] retention / retribution / restitution / retaliation

Corrigé

[1] scope. « fall within the scope of » = entrer dans le champ d'application.
[2] baseline. « against a 2023 baseline » = par rapport à l'année de référence 2023. « bottom line » désigne le résultat net.
[3] offsetting. « offsetting » = compensation carbone.
[4] faith. Expression figée : « in good faith » (de bonne foi).
[5] retaliation. « protected against retaliation » = protégé contre les représailles. « restitution » signifie remboursement, restitution.

Exercice 11 — C1-M3-Q11 (C2, C1.1)

Complétez l'extrait de rapport d'audit avec le terme qui convient.

We provide [1] _____ assurance. In 6 of the 25 payments [2] _____, there was no evidence of independent review. The [3] _____ cause is a lack of segregation of [4] _____. Management's response was partially [5] _____.

[1] limitless / limiting / limited / limitative

[2] simulated / sampled / sampling / assembled

[3] root / roots / rooted / route

[4] charges / tasks / jobs / duties

[5] agreement / agreeing / agreed / agreeable

Corrigé

[1] limited. « limited assurance » = niveau d'opinion défavorable dans l'échelle d'assurance.
[2] sampled. « payments sampled » = opérations de l'échantillon (participe passé à valeur passive).
[3] root. « root cause » = cause racine. « route » est un homophone fréquent dans les fautes.
[4] duties. Collocation figée : « segregation of duties ».
[5] agreed. « partially agreed » = acceptée en partie, mention standard de la réponse de la direction.

Exercice 12 — C1-M3-Q12 (C2, C1.2)

Complétez cette note de synthèse comparant deux sources avec le terme qui convient.

The supplier's reply seeks to [1] _____ blame onto the haulier, and its claim that monitoring worked is not [2] _____ by the customer's data. There is a [3] _____ between the two delivery times reported, which can only be [4] _____ if the transfer time is excluded. The customer's tone, though polite, contains a [5] _____ warning.

[1] reflect / deflect / inflect / defer

[2] corroborated / corrected / correlated / co-operated

[3] disclosure / discrimination / discount / discrepancy

[4] reconditioned / recommended / reconciled / recollected

[5] valid / veiled / vented / vetted

Corrigé

[1] deflect. « deflect blame onto » = rejeter la responsabilité sur. « defer » signifie reporter.
[2] corroborated. « not corroborated by » = non confirmé par.
[3] discrepancy. « discrepancy between two figures » = écart, incohérence.
[4] reconciled. « can only be reconciled if » = ne peuvent être conciliés que si.
[5] veiled. « a veiled warning » = un avertissement voilé. « vetted » signifie contrôlé, validé.

sections.title: Mise en situation : Note d'analyse critique d'un dossier documentaire de mon secteur
sections.contentHtml:
Compétence C2 — 40 min

Votre direction vous demande de préparer, avant une réunion stratégique, une analyse critique d'un dossier de deux ou trois documents en anglais portant sur un même sujet (par exemple : extrait de rapport annuel d'un concurrent + article de presse sur ses résultats ; politique ESG d'un fournisseur + communiqué d'une ONG ; conditions générales d'un prestataire + courriel de votre service juridique). Le formateur fournit un dossier original ; vous pouvez aussi utiliser des documents publics de votre secteur, à condition de les anonymiser. Pour chaque document, complétez la grille d'analyse : émetteur et intérêt, type de document, thèse ou objet, trois informations clés, attitude de l'auteur justifiée par une citation, deux éléments implicites (euphémisme, litote, omission, condition). Rédigez ensuite, en anglais, une note de synthèse de 150 à 200 mots qui identifie au moins une convergence, une divergence et une omission entre les sources, et formule une conclusion prudente.

Livrable : Grille d'analyse complétée pour chaque document + note de synthèse en anglais (150–200 mots), déposées dans l'espace de dépôt du module.

Critères d'évaluation :

  • L'émetteur et son intérêt sont correctement identifiés pour chaque document.
  • L'attitude de chaque auteur est qualifiée avec précision et justifiée par une citation exacte.
  • Au moins deux éléments implicites par document sont repérés et reformulés en langage direct.
  • La synthèse distingue clairement les faits, les interprétations et les opinions rapportées.
  • Au moins une convergence, une divergence et une omission entre les sources sont identifiées.
  • La note en anglais emploie le lexique de la comparaison (corroborate, diverge, discrepancy, unlike…) avec un niveau de langue C1.
  • Aucune conclusion n'est plus catégorique que ce que les sources permettent d'affirmer.

title: C1-M4 — Construire une argumentation : claim, evidence, rebuttal
description: Formuler en une phrase une thèse (claim) précise, délimitée et défendable sur un sujet professionnel. Appuyer chaque thèse sur au moins deux éléments de preuve de nature différente (chiffre, exemple, référence) reliés explicitement à la thèse par un raisonnement (warrant). Anticiper une objection et y répondre (rebuttal) dans une intervention orale de 90 à 120 secondes, sans hésitation notable.
